analysis.one_liner: Bans health insurers and employers from discriminating against people based on their genetic information.
analysis.headline: The bill became law: the House passed it 420-3, the Senate passed it 95-0, and the President signed it on May 21, 2008.
analysis.plain_summary: The law makes it illegal for health insurers to deny coverage, set premiums, or impose preexisting-condition exclusions based on genetic test results or family medical history, and illegal for employers to hire, fire, or assign workers based on the same information. It also bars insurers from requiring genetic tests and extends medical privacy rules to genetic information. A separate section raises federal fines for employers who violate child labor and minimum wage rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who has taken a genetic test, has a family history of a disease, or might want genetic testing or genetic counseling in the future. Before this law, a positive test result or a family disease history could be used by insurers to deny coverage or raise premiums, and by employers to make hiring and firing decisions. The bill's own findings say the fear of such discrimination was keeping people from getting genetic testing that could catch diseases early [S6]. People with conditions that run in families, and members of groups disproportionately affected by certain genetic conditions, gain the most [S6].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with genetic risks or family disease history

how_it_helps.text: Health insurers in both the group and individual markets can no longer deny coverage, raise premiums, or apply preexisting-condition exclusions based on genetic information, and cannot require anyone to take a genetic test [S3] [S5].

Employers, employment agencies, labor organizations, and training programs cannot hire, fire, classify, or discriminate against workers because of genetic information, and cannot request or purchase employees' genetic information outside narrow exceptions [S3] [S5].
Genetic information gets the same privacy protections as other health information, and insurers are barred from using it for underwriting purposes [S3] [S5].

The bill's findings state that a national uniform standard was needed because the patchwork of state laws varied widely and was inadequate, and that relieving the fear of discrimination would allow people to take advantage of genetic testing and new therapies [S6].

The Senate version added higher federal penalties for employers who violate child labor rules, including a new penalty for violations causing the death or serious injury of a worker under 18, and higher maximum penalties for repeat or willful minimum wage and overtime violations [S4] [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers bear the compliance costs and lose the ability to price coverage or make employment decisions using genetic risk information. Insurers can still price based on a disease that has actually manifested, so the cost of risk does not disappear, but it is spread across policyholders rather than concentrated on people with genetic markers [S3] [S5].

drawbacks.text: The law does not create a 'disparate impact' cause of action, so a practice that screens out people with certain genetic traits without targeting them by name is not actionable; a study commission was set up six years after enactment just to consider whether to add one [S3] [S5].
Insurers and employers can still use the manifestation of a disease once symptoms appear, so once a genetic risk becomes a diagnosed illness, the old rules can apply again [S5].

Penalties for group health plans that violate the genetic rules include broad waivers, caps, and reduced minimums for failures due to reasonable cause, and the law allows insurers to request voluntary genetic tests for research purposes as long as results are not used for underwriting [S5].

Employers keep several exceptions to the ban on acquiring genetic information, including wellness programs with voluntary written authorization, genetic monitoring of toxic-substance exposure, and forensic DNA work [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a real civil-rights protection: before this law, a person who learned they carried a gene for a serious disease risked losing their health coverage or their job over it, and the fear alone deterred people from tests that can catch disease early [S6]. The cost falls on insurers and employers, who lose an underwriting and screening tool, with compliance burdens for maintaining separate confidential files. The main design weakness is enforcement: no disparate-impact claims, waivers and caps on plan penalties, and a bright line at 'manifestation' that lets discrimination restart once a disease is diagnosed [S3] [S5]. On balance it is a strong, if imperfect, protection for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 420-3 in April 2007, the Senate sat on it for nearly a year before passing it 95-0 in April 2008 with an amendment, the House agreed to that amendment 414-1, and President Bush signed it into law on May 21, 2008.

narrative.text: Introduced by Rep. Louise Slaughter in January 2007, the bill was considered by three House committees — Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, and Ways and Means — and reported by all three in late March 2007 [S8].

The House passed it on April 25, 2007 under a suspension-of-the-rules vote (a fast-track procedure requiring a two-thirds majority and no amendments), 420-3, with 229 of 231 Democrats and 191 of 201 Republicans in favor [S8] [S9].

The Senate received the bill in April 2007 but it sat on the Senate calendar for nearly a year before being brought up by unanimous consent on April 24, 2008, when it passed 95-0 with an amendment [S8] [S10].
The House agreed to the Senate amendment on May 1, 2008 by a vote of 414-1, and President Bush signed it on May 21, 2008 as Public Law 110-233 [S8] [S11].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people with genetic risk factors came out ahead: they gained a federal guarantee that their DNA and family medical history cannot be used against them in health insurance or employment. The genetic testing and research field also gained, since the bill's stated purpose was to remove the fear of discrimination so people would take advantage of genetic testing and new therapies [S6].

sides.party_line_note: The bill was overwhelmingly bipartisan at every stage: 224 cosponsors split 129 Democrats and 95 Republicans, the House passed it 420-3 with all but 3 Republicans and all Democrats in favor, and the Senate passed it 95-0 with every senator voting in support [S7] [S9] [S10].

industries.note: The law bars insurers from using genetic information for underwriting — denying coverage, setting premiums, or applying preexisting-condition exclusions — and from requiring genetic tests, in both group and individual markets, including Medicare supplemental (medigap) policies [S3] [S5]. They remain the gatekeepers of coverage and can still price based on manifested disease, but lose a screening tool whose use would have shifted costs onto genetically vulnerable people [S5].

Employers lose the ability to acquire or act on employees' genetic information in hiring and employment decisions, and must keep any genetic data in separate confidential files. They retain exceptions for wellness programs, workplace toxic-exposure monitoring, and forensic DNA work, and the Senate version raised penalties on them for child labor and wage violations [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Genetic testing and genetic services industry
industries.note: The bill's findings state that relieving the fear of discrimination will let individuals take advantage of genetic testing, technologies, research, and new therapies [S6]. By guaranteeing that a test result cannot cost someone their coverage or job, the law removes the main deterrent to buying genetic tests and counseling.
